tasks.knowledge_enhanced_prompt:
## Relevant Domain Knowledge

**BESS Energy Accounting**
- Usable capacity: SOC_max − SOC_min = (0.80 − 0.20) × 500 kWh = 300 kWh
- Initial usable energy above minimum: (0.50 − 0.20) × 500 = 150 kWh
- Charging (grid → battery): Energy stored = P_charge × η_one-way; η_one-way = √0.90 ≈ 0.9487
- Discharging (battery → grid): Energy delivered = P_discharge × η_one-way; energy removed from battery = P_discharge / η_one-way
- SOC update (charging): SOC_new = SOC_prev + (P_charge × η_one-way) / 500
- SOC update (discharging): SOC_new = SOC_prev − (P_discharge / η_one-way) / 500
- Power limits: 0 ≤ P_charge ≤ 250 kW; 0 ≤ P_discharge ≤ 250 kW; mutually exclusive per hour

**Revenue Calculation**
- Revenue per hour ($) = [P_solar_export + P_discharge] × Price($/MWh) × (1 h / 1000 kW·h per MWh) − [P_charge] × Price($/MWh) × (1/1000)
- Grid export from solar = Solar(kW) when battery is not being charged from solar (solar surplus goes to grid)
- When charging from grid: cost = P_charge × Price / 1000
- Net revenue = Σ_h [ (Solar_h + P_discharge_h − P_charge_h) × Price_h / 1000 ]

**Optimal Dispatch Strategy (Price Arbitrage)**
- Charge during lowest-price hours; discharge during highest-price hours
- Profit per kWh cycled = Price_discharge × η_RT − Price_charge, where η_RT = 0.90
- Arbitrage is profitable when: Price_discharge / Price_charge > 1/η_RT = 1/0.90 ≈ 1.111
- Solar energy: always export to grid (zero marginal cost); opportunity exists to store solar only if future price > current price / η_one-way
- Charge rate limited to 250 kW; full charge from min to max = 300 kWh / η_one-way = 316.2 kWh input energy, requiring ≥ 2 hours at 250 kW (250 × 0.9487 = 237.2 kWh stored/hr)

**Unit Conversions**
- Power (kW) × Time (1 h) = Energy (kWh)
- Revenue ($) = Energy (kWh) × Price ($/MWh) × (1 MWh / 1000 kWh) = kW × Price / 1000

**SOC Constraint Enforcement**
- Stored energy must remain within [100 kWh, 400 kWh] (i.e., [20%, 80%] × 500 kWh)
- Maximum discharge energy deliverable in one hour: min(250, (SOC_stored − 100) × η_one-way) kWh
- Maximum charge energy absorbable in one hour: min(250 × η_one-way, 400 − SOC_stored) kWh stored

tasks.knowledge_enhanced_prompt:
## Domain Knowledge

**Energy Required per Group**
$$E_{\text{required}} = N \times C_{\text{batt}} \times (\text{SOC}_{\text{target}} - \text{SOC}_{\text{arrival}})$$
where $C_{\text{batt}} = 60\text{ kWh}$, SOC values are fractional.

**Maximum Power per Group (all EVs charging simultaneously)**
$$P_{\text{group,max}} = N \times P_{\text{charger}}$$

**Minimum Hours Required per Group (charging at full rate)**
$$t_{\text{min}} = \left\lceil \frac{E_{\text{required}}}{P_{\text{group,max}}} \right\rceil \text{ hours}$$
i.e., the group must charge for at least this many hours within its parking window.

**Parking Window (available hours)**
Each group can only draw power during hours $[\text{arrival}, \text{departure})$. Fractional scheduling within an hour is permitted (a group can charge at full rate for a fraction of an hour), but for peak-demand minimization the standard approach is to treat each clock-hour as a scheduling slot and allow partial loading within a slot.

**Grid Connection Constraint**
$$\sum_{\text{groups } g} P_{g,h} \leq 500\text{ kW} \quad \forall h$$

**Per-Group Power Constraint**
$$0 \leq P_{g,h} \leq P_{\text{group,max},g} \quad \forall g, h$$

**Energy Fulfillment Constraint**
$$\sum_{h \in \text{window}_g} P_{g,h} \cdot \Delta t = E_{\text{required},g}, \quad \Delta t = 1\text{ h}$$

**Peak Demand Minimization Objective**
$$\min \; D_{\text{peak}}, \quad \text{where } D_{\text{peak}} = \max_h \sum_g P_{g,h}$$

This is a linear program (LP): minimize $D$ subject to $\sum_g P_{g,h} \leq D$ for all $h$, plus energy and power constraints.

**Key Group Parameters (pre-computed for reference)**

| Group | N | $P_{\text{max}}$ (kW) | $E_{\text{req}}$ (kWh) | Window (hrs) | $t_{\text{min}}$ (hrs) |
|-------|---|-----------------------|------------------------|--------------|------------------------|
| A | 20 | 144 | 600 | 07–17 (10 h) | 5 |
| B | 15 | 108 | 450 | 08–16 (8 h) | 5 |
| C | 10 | 110 | 360 | 09–18 (9 h) | 4 |
| D | 5  | 55  | 90  | 07–12 (5 h) | 2 |

**Lower Bound on Peak Demand**
The tightest lower bound is the maximum over all hours of the minimum power that *must* flow. A useful bound is:
$$D_{\text{peak}} \geq \max_g \frac{E_{\text{required},g}}{|\text{window}_g|}$$
and also $D_{\text{peak}} \geq \frac{\sum_g E_{\text{required},g}}{|\text{union of all windows}|}$.

Total energy = $600 + 450 + 360 + 90 = 1500\text{ kWh}$ over the span 07:00–18:00 (11 hours), giving a global lower bound of $1500/11 \approx 136.4\text{ kW}$.

tasks.knowledge_enhanced_prompt:
## Domain Knowledge

**BESS Round-Trip Efficiency:**
Round-trip efficiency (RTE) = η_RT = 92% = η_charge × η_discharge. Commonly modeled as symmetric: η_charge = η_discharge = √0.92 ≈ 0.9592. Energy delivered on discharge = Energy charged × η_RT. Effective cost of arbitrage cycle per kWh discharged: buy price / η_RT + degradation_discharge + degradation_charge.

**Arbitrage Profit per kWh discharged:**
Profit_arbitrage = P_discharge − (P_charge / η_RT) − C_deg × (1/η_charge + 1) [in $/kWh]
where C_deg = $0.02/kWh applies to both charge throughput and discharge throughput separately.
Total degradation per full cycle (1 kWh discharged): $0.02 (charge) + $0.02 (discharge) = $0.04/kWh discharged, plus the efficiency loss: effective charge cost = P_charge / η_RT.
Net arbitrage spread required to break even: ΔP_min = P_charge/η_RT − P_charge + $0.04/kWh × 1000 = P_charge×(1/0.92−1) + $40/MWh.

**Frequency Regulation Revenue:**
- Capacity payment (reg-up): $15/MW·h — paid on committed MW regardless of dispatch.
- Capacity payment (reg-down): $12/MW·h — paid on committed MW regardless of dispatch.
- Expected energy throughput from regulation calls: utilization rate × committed capacity × 15 min/60 min = 0.20 × C_reg × 0.25 h per hour.
- Expected energy dispatched per hour (reg-up): 0.20 × C_reg_up × 0.25 MWh (discharge).
- Expected energy dispatched per hour (reg-down): 0.20 × C_reg_down × 0.25 MWh (charge).
- Degradation cost from regulation dispatch: $0.02/kWh × expected throughput (both charge and discharge events).
- Net regulation revenue per MW committed per hour:
  - Reg-up: $15/MW·h − $0.02/kWh × 0.20 × 0.25 h × 1000 kWh/MWh = $15 − $1.00 = $14.00/MW·h (net of degradation, excluding energy settlement).
  - Reg-down: $12/MW·h − $0.02/kWh × 0.20 × 0.25 h × 1000 kWh/MWh = $12 − $1.00 = $11.00/MW·h (net of degradation).
- Energy settlement for regulation calls (if applicable): reg-up dispatch is paid at real-time price ≈ day-ahead price; reg-down dispatch costs the day-ahead price.

**BESS Physical Constraints:**
- Power: 0 ≤ P_charge(t) + P_reg_down_reserved(t) ≤ 500 kW; 0 ≤ P_discharge(t) + P_reg_up_reserved(t) ≤ 500 kW.
- Energy: SOC(t) ∈ [0, 1 MWh] (0–100%).
- SOC update: SOC(t+1) = SOC(t) − P_discharge(t)×Δt/η_discharge + P_charge(t)×η_charge×Δt, Δt = 1 h.
- Capacity committed to regulation-up must be backed by available stored energy: C_reg_up(t) × 0.25 h ≤ SOC(t) (worst-case 15-min full delivery).
- Capacity committed to regulation-down must be backed by available headroom: C_reg_down(t) × 0.25 h ≤ 1 MWh − SOC(t).
- Total power allocation: P_arb_discharge(t) + C_reg_up(t) ≤ 500 kW; P_arb_charge(t) + C_reg_down(t) ≤ 500 kW.

**Curtailable Load:**
- Available 200 kW of curtailable industrial load can be offered as a demand response resource in the energy market (equivalent to generation): revenue = curtailment × Δt × P_DA(t), subject to contractual limits (assume fully available each hour unless otherwise stated).

**Opportunity Cost Framework:**
For each hour t, the marginal value of allocating 1 MW of BESS to regulation vs. arbitrage:
- Value of reg-up per MW·h = $14.00 + 0.20 × 0.25 × P_DA(t) [capacity payment net degradation + expected energy revenue]
- Value of reg-down per MW·h = $11.00 − 0.20 × 0.25 × P_DA(t) [capacity payment net degradation − expected energy cost]
- Arbitrage is only profitable when spread P_discharge − P_charge/η_RT > $40/MWh (break-even spread).

A residential neighborhood contains 155 single-family homes. Each home has central air conditioning (average 3.1 kW nameplate, typical duty cycle 60%), a smart water heater (5.0 kW, can be curtailed for up to 2.5 hours without comfort impact), and a pool pump where applicable (1.4 kW, 35% of homes have pools, typically run 5 hours/day). The utility wants to dispatch a demand response event during a summer afternoon peak (1 PM–3 PM). Assume 65% of AC units are actively cycling at any given moment during peak, 80% customer participation rate, and that pool pumps can be fully curtailed during the 2-hour window. Estimate the aggregate demand response potential (kW sheddable sustained for 2 hours) and explain your methodology step by step.
tasks.knowledge_enhanced_prompt:
## Domain Knowledge

**Demand Response (DR) Sheddable Load Definitions**
- *Sheddable sustained load*: the portion of load that can be curtailed continuously for the specified duration (here, 2 hours) without violating comfort, safety, or equipment constraints.
- Aggregate DR potential (kW) = Σ [Device_i × Participation_Rate_i × Diversity_Factor_i × Duty_Cycle_i × Rated_Power_i]

**Key Device Parameters & Standard Assumptions**
- **HVAC (central A/C):** Typical residential unit: 3–5 ton (3.5 kW–5.8 kW per ton; 1 ton = 3.517 kW). Duty cycle during peak summer: 60–80%. DR sheddable fraction: up to 100% of runtime power for short events; for 2-hour sustained events, assume 50% duty-cycle reduction is feasible without exceeding ±2°F comfort band (ASHRAE Standard 55 thermal comfort). Effective sheddable power = Rated_kW × Duty_Cycle × Curtailment_Fraction.
- **Electric Water Heater (EWH):** Typical element: 4.5 kW (240 V, ~18.75 A). Duty cycle: 20–30% at peak. Full element can be shed for 2 hours using thermal storage in tank (standard 40–80 gal tank retains heat ~2–4 hours per DOE test procedure 10 CFR Part 430). Sheddable fraction: ~100% of duty-cycle power.
- **EV Charger (Level 2):** Typical: 7.2 kW (240 V, 30 A). Fully deferrable if battery SOC > 20% and departure time > 2 hours away. Participation rate depends on time-of-day and SOC distribution.
- **Pool Pump:** Typical: 1–2 kW (variable speed) to 2–3 kW (single speed). Fully sheddable for 2 hours with no comfort impact. Participation rate ~80–90% in DR programs (CPUC and FERC Order 2222 experience).
- **Clothes Dryer / Dishwasher:** Interruptible but low coincidence factor at any given hour; typically excluded from sustained 2-hour DR estimates unless specifically scheduled.

**Diversity Factor**
- Diversity Factor (DF) accounts for the fact that not all devices are operating simultaneously.
- DF = Maximum Coincident Demand / Sum of Individual Maximum Demands.
- Typical residential cluster DF for HVAC: 0.70–0.85 (summer peak); EWH: 0.25–0.40; EV: 0.30–0.60 (evening peak).

**Participation Rate**
- Voluntary DR programs: 40–60% opt-in rate (SERC/NERC DR survey data).
- Automated/utility-controlled (e.g., smart thermostat, direct load control): 70–90%.

**Unit Conversions & Standards**
- 1 ton cooling = 3.517 kW electrical (at standard EER/COP assumptions).
- IEEE 1815 (DNP3) and OpenADR 2.0b govern signaling for automated DR dispatch.
- FERC Order 2222: aggregated DERs ≥ 100 kW may participate in wholesale markets.
- Baseline for DR measurement: NERC/FERC define sheddable kW relative to the Customer Baseline Load (CBL), typically a 10-of-10 day average.

tasks.knowledge_enhanced_prompt:
## Domain Knowledge

**Demand Response (DR) Fundamentals:**
- Load reduction (kWh) = Baseline load (kW) × Duration (h) × Participation rate × Average % reduction per event
- Annual load reduction (MWh) = Load reduction per event (kWh) × Number of events per year / 1000
- Cost-effectiveness ratio = Total utility cost ($) / Total load reduction (MWh)
- Customer bill savings = Incentive payments received − any inconvenience costs

**Baseline Load Calculation:**
- Residential baseline typically uses a 10-of-10 method: average of the 10 highest-use days in the preceding 30 days (FERC-accepted standard)
- Typical residential peak load: 3–6 kW per household during summer peak hours (2–7 PM)

**Incentive Program Types (FERC Order 2222 / IEEE 2030.x context):**
- **Direct Load Control (DLC):** Utility controls devices directly (e.g., smart thermostats, water heaters); typical participation rate 60–80%; customer acceptance moderate
- **Price-Based DR (TOU/CPP):** Customers respond voluntarily to price signals; typical participation rate 20–45%; elasticity of demand typically −0.05 to −0.20 for residential customers
- **Incentive-Based DR:** Fixed or event-based payments; typical participation rate 40–70%

**Cost-Effectiveness Metrics:**
- Utility Avoided Cost: Typically $50–$150/MWh for avoided peak energy; $50,000–$150,000/MW-year for avoided capacity
- Program Cost = Incentive payments + Administrative overhead (typically 15–25% of incentive budget)
- Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR) = (Avoided energy cost + Avoided capacity cost) / Total program cost; BCR > 1.0 indicates cost-effective program
- California Standard Practice Manual (CSPM) defines TRC (Total Resource Cost) and PAC (Program Administrator Cost) tests for DR cost-effectiveness

**Customer Experience Metrics:**
- Customer Satisfaction Score (CSS) inversely correlated with event frequency and control intrusiveness
- Opt-out rate benchmarks: DLC programs ~5–15% opt-out per event; voluntary price programs ~10–30% non-response
- Comfort penalty index: Each degree of thermostat setback ≈ 3–5% load reduction but reduces satisfaction by ~0.3 points per °F on a 10-point scale
- Customer retention in DR programs: ~70–85% year-over-year for well-designed incentive programs

**Unit Conversions & Standards:**
- 1 MW = 1,000 kW; 1 MWh = 1,000 kWh
- Peak demand period: typically 4–6 hours per event
- NERC defines DR performance ratio = Actual reduction / Nominated reduction; target ≥ 0.90 for reliable programs

tasks.knowledge_enhanced_prompt:
## Domain Knowledge

**Energy-arbitrage revenue:** delivered MWh times the energy price, minus throughput-based degradation (throughput in kWh times the $/kWh rate).

**Regulation-up revenue stack:** a capacity payment (offered MW times the $/MW-hr rate, paid regardless of calls) plus an energy settlement (expected utilization fraction times offered MWh times the real-time settlement price), minus degradation on the *expected* discharged throughput only.

**Break-even price:** set the two net-revenue expressions equal and solve for the energy price - only the day-ahead leg depends on it, so the equation is linear in the price.
